The Armenian Kings.
{she gave?} consent for her sake.
And she, when she heard,
was agitated, and began wailing, insulting, and scorning Bahram.
Then noble men and noble women persuaded her,
saying, "For the sake of your son's welfare, even to fire you should surrender yourself."
And so against her will she consented, while crying out:
"This is forced fornication for me,
and not a lawful marriage."
And when Bahram took her as a wife, he magnified her honor,
and went to serve her and her son.
And he encamped against the city of Tarsus and took it.
And from there he went to Adana,
and took it also.
And he went again against Mopsuestia.
And while they were encamped against it,
the famous Baron Constantine gathered an army,
and went against them and struck them.
And when they fled before him,
he pursued them, and he drove {them} {OCR?} and shut them up in the city of Tarsus.
And there he captured and destroyed them all:
Bahram, and Rupen, and his mother, the daughter of Rupen the Great.
And from then on, that famous one expected the Armenian grandees to tell him
to take the daughter of King Leo for one of his sons and make him king,
because he had five sons.
And when this was not told to him,
he was offended in his mind,
and conducted himself craftily with them.
And they sent and brought Philip, the son of the Blind Prince,
and gave him Isabel, the daughter of King Leo,
and made him king over Cilicia.
And he ruled for about two years or more, but in a corrupt manner.
For he purposed to destroy all the Armenian grandees,
and to appoint Franks in their place.
And he began to despise the Armenians,
and instead of "soldiers" he used to call them "laborers,"
and he would not permit them to eat with him at his table.
And when they came ten times to his gate,
hardly once would he command that they enter before him.
And thus his hatred grew strong against the Armenians.
And when they could no longer endure his tyranny,
they gathered to the famous Baron Constantine,
and besought him to devise for them a deliverance from him,
since they deeply regretted having made him king.
